title: The one dear to me
hookLine: Krishna ends the chapter on devotion with a portrait, not a ritual
carry: free from hate, friendly to all
last: THE LADDER — EVERY RUNG REACHES GOD.

lines: THE FRIEND WHO HOLDS NO GRUDGES.
cards: There's a kind of friend who doesn't hold grudges. Who's the same at a wedding and a hospital. Who doesn't need anyone to agree with them.
People leave their kitchen lighter than they came in, and nobody's quite sure how. Chapter twelve is the chapter of bhakti, devotion.
You might expect it to end with instructions: which offering, which mantra, how many times. It doesn't. It ends with a portrait of a person.
Eight verses, and a refrain that keeps coming back.

teach.b: Verse thirteen opens the portrait. The one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of mine and free of ego, the same in pleasure and pain, forgiving.

The Sanskrit starts adveshta sarva-bhutanam: without hatred toward all beings. Then maitra, friendly, and karuna, compassion. Again and again the verses close with some version of the same small phrase: sa me priyah.
That one is dear to me. It's Krishna's voice, and it's tender. Verse fifteen turns it both ways: the world does not shrink from them, and they do not shrink from the world.
Nobody is afraid of them, and they aren't afraid of anybody. The portrait keeps going. Not elated, not hating, not grieving, not craving.

teach.h: THE SAME IN HONOR AND INSULT.
teach.b: The same to friend and enemy, in honor and insult, in cold and heat. Quiet. Content with whatever comes.

And a surprising word in verse nineteen: aniketa, without a fixed home. Commentators read it as someone who doesn't cling to their house as the center of the universe, not necessarily someone homeless.
Notice what isn't on the list. No rank. No caste.
No particular ritual. The chapter on devotion ends by describing how a devoted person treats everyone else.

teach.h: THAT ONE IS DEAR TO ME.
teach.b: Verse twenty closes it: those who follow this with faith are exceedingly dear.
That closes the chapter, and the week. It started with the vision that shook Arjuna, and it ends with a kind face.

how: Gita chapter twelve, the chapter of bhakti, is short, and many Hindus memorize or recite it; its closing verses (12.13–12.20) are often read as a description of the devotee's character.

o: chosen and set apart above all others
dear and beloved, held close to the heart
pure and spotless, free from any fault

s: the chapter on devotion ends with a list of rituals
it ends with a portrait of a person: free of hate, friendly, the same in honor and insult.
verse 15 says no one is afraid of this person, and they aren't afraid of anyone
the world doesn't shrink from them, and they don't shrink from the world.

games.q: you've reached the end of the chapter on devotion. what does Krishna finish with?
o: the right offerings and their times.
a portrait of how the devoted person treats everyone.
a warning to those who don't worship.
games.why: a portrait. eight verses on character, with the refrain 'that one is dear to me' coming back again and again.

practice: Recall one recent moment of praise and one of criticism, a compliment and a sharp word, and hold each for a breath, noticing what happens in you.
Then, for a few breaths, let both sit side by side: the same in honor and insult, as verse eighteen puts it. You don't have to feel nothing; just stay even.

wordCard.voice: Priya, dear, beloved. Gita twelve, thirteen to twenty: a portrait of the devoted person, free of hate, friendly and kind, and the refrain, sa me priyah, that one is dear to me.

orig.note: Sanskrit: priya, dear, beloved; the refrain 'sa me priyah', that one is dear to me.

carryVoice: Your line: free from hate, friendly to all. The vision in chapter eleven, form or formless, the ladder, the portrait: that's the week.
